title: Trump’s Attempts to Control the Census: Your Questions Answered
author: Ask Bolts
content:
The Trump administration
[plans](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/04/donald-trump-2030-census-
changes-01104876) to upend the census. They’re proposing to [exclude
noncitizens](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-5845147/trump-us-census-
citizenship-question-race-categories) from the count that determines the
distribution of congressional seats, a move that would subtract political
power from regions with large immigrant populations. They also want to stop
collecting data about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

Their efforts are a stark reminder of how much the census shapes our politics.
Its results guide redistricting, apportion congressional districts, and steer
government funding—processes that are vulnerable to decisions made by public
officials on how to collect and organize the data.

Last month, we invited _Bolts_ readers to send us questions about the census
and the latest proposals to transform it.

Then, we shared many of those questions with danah boyd, an ethnographer and
professor of communication who wrote a new book on the census, “[Data Are
Made, Not
Found](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/D/bo277581183.html).”
boyd interviewed hundreds of civil servants who worked on the 2020 census as
they dealt with major obstacles including budget constraints and the COVID-19
pandemic.

The 2020 census proved challenging enough, but boyd shares her worries about
what lies ahead. “Right now, the Census Bureau is facing the destruction of
long-standing norms, the departure of people with sizable institutional
knowledge, micromanaging of the scientific method, and egregious partisan
dictates,” she told _Bolts_.

She explains why she thinks it’s risky for the Census Bureau to start asking
people about their citizenship, and what would be lost if it stops collecting
data about race. And she lays out why it might be hard to roll back some of
the decisions the Trump administration is making right now—unless Congress
intervenes soon.

boyd answers 10 questions here. Select the one you are most interested in from
the list below, or keep scrolling to explore them all.

**Is the census based on the whims of the current administration or is it
intended to count all people living in the country as of a particular date? I
always thought all residents were supposed to be counted, based on my mom’s
experience as a census worker in 1960._— Flicker, from Oregon_**

In the United States, the census is the backbone of our representative
democracy. After establishing the existence of a Congress, the Constitution
explains in Article 1, Section 2 that representatives shall be apportioned
among the states “according to their respective Numbers” which are to be
enumerated by processes set forth by Congress. The clause contains a horrific
stain on our country’s history because non-“free” persons are to only be
counted as three-fifths of a person; this was corrected by the Fourteenth
Amendment. But it is also clear that everyone is to be counted. And that
Congress is responsible for the census.

Since the first census in 1790, all people who are residents of the United
States have been counted, regardless of where they are born or if they were
formally naturalized. In modern times, the “residence rules” for the census
have excluded people who are tourists visiting the U.S. or diplomats from
other countries, but they have never excluded people who call the U.S. their
home. The pressure to exclude non-citizens from apportionment is a partisan
move that is decades in the making, rooted deeply in a xenophobic and
isolationist history.

For a good overall history of the census, I highly recommend [Margo Anderson’s
“The American Census.”](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300195422/the-
american-census/)

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/7024456499_1c8f36c64e_o-2400x1700.jpg)1940 census
workers transferring data to punch cards. (U.S. Census Bureau/Flickr)

  
**Since there are and have always been political implications, have presidents interfered in the past by “ordering” the Census Bureau to count or not count people?_— JCreek, from California_ | How have particular administrations tried to limit or manipulate representation of people of color? _— Anonymous, from Los Angeles  _**

The Constitution tasks Congress with running the census. [After the 1920
census](https://knightcolumbia.org/content/democracys-data-infrastructure),
Southern Democrats were afraid that they were going to lose political power
once reapportionment happened so they refused to reapportion, arguing that
they could only do so once they figured out the “right” math. [By
1929](https://datasociety.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/House-Arrest-Dan-
Bouk.pdf), Congress still hadn’t reapportioned the House (although Southern
Democrats had managed to pass a lot of anti-immigration laws in an effort to
reduce their loss of power). Frustrated, a group of senators pushed through
the “Permanent Reapportionment Act of 1929.”

One of the weird artifacts of this law is that Congress instructed the
president to convert census data into seats in the House of Representatives
out of fear that political infighting would prevent Congress from doing its
job. The idea was that the president wouldn’t mess with reapportionment like
Congress had. And until President Trump tried to mess with this process in the
2020 census, no president had interfered at this level.

The pressure to not count non-citizens is not actually new. [John
Tanton](https://www.npr.org/2021/02/15/967783477/immigration-hard-liner-files-
reveal-40-year-bid-behind-trumps-census-obsession) pushed to prevent the
Census Bureau from counting non-citizens decades ago. His legal efforts
failed; the courts repeatedly ruled that the census must count everyone. But
that didn’t stop his network of people from continuing to try. This is the
backstory to President Trump’s efforts.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/26010000594277-scaled.jpg)Two young children hold
signs through the car window at an outreach event in Dallas for the 2020 U.S.
Census. (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez, File)

  
**Why would Trump and his allies want to ask about citizenship on the census?
What could they stand to gain?_— Bolts staff_**

The first Trump administration tried but failed to introduce a citizenship
question in the 2020 decennial census. Keep in mind that citizenship is
already asked about a sample of the population for the American Community
Survey (ACS); the goal was to collect this data about the _entire_ population,
not just those who responded to the ACS. As the story unfolded, three
motivations emerged. The publicly stated reason by the Trump administration
was that they needed this data to enforce the Voting Rights Act (VRA). That’s
peculiar because 1) the VRA has been enforced for decades without having this
data; 2) VRA compliance has long been done using the ACS; and 3) the Trump
administration was opposed to the VRA.

Another motivation was clearly the result of a court case known as _Evenwel v.
Abbott_ , where the Supreme Court gave states the opportunity to draw
districts using citizenship data. Some redistricters argued that having this
about the whole population would make for more effective redistricting than
using just the data collected by the ACS.

A third motivation was only presumed but not explicitly known until late in
the first Trump administration. In short, President Trump wanted to subtract
certain classes of non-citizens from the apportionment base before turning the
results over to Congress. The administration made this goal explicit late in
2020, but it was not implemented after President Trump lost his bid for re-
election.

The second Trump administration is
[returning](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/10/2026-18481/decennial-
census-of-the-population-of-americans-proposed-residence-criteria-and-
proposed-regulations) to the citizenship question. It is both requiring the
question and planning to simply not collect data about certain non-citizens,
thereby undermining the population count at the counting stage and making it
impossible to repair down the line. We are bound to see significant legal
challenges to this.

Keep in mind that, even if Congress did pass a law ordering the bureau not to
count non-citizens, the Supreme Court would have to decide if excluding non-
citizens from the apportionment base violates Article 1, Section 2 of the
Constitution. Most legal scholars (and previous court rulings like _Franklin
v. Massachusetts_) argue it does. But this Supreme Court has already upended
precedent in peculiar ways, so it is unclear how they would rule.

  
**With this citizenship question, would they expect enumerators to confirm
citizenship? Will people really dig out their passports and birth certificates
to show an enumerator?_— JCreek, from California_**

People do lie on the census, intentionally and inadvertently. They lie about
every variable, regardless of how significant it is. I’m always humored by
how, since at least 1880, a sizable enough number of people lie about their
age that, if the Census Bureau were to publish age data as collected, you’d
get insane heaps around ages ending in ‘0’ and ‘5.’

Data are not published as collected; [they are
made](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/D/bo277581183.html).
And there are many different ways to address errors in the collected data,
including triangulating with other sources like administrative data. So even
if people “lied” about their citizenship status, data from Homeland Security
might be used to “fix” the data. However, I’m putting these words in
quotations because Homeland Security does not always have more accurate data,
especially about newly naturalized citizens. The bureau also knows that the
administrative data that they get often have a delay on them; people are
citizens but the records say that they are not-yet citizens. Our data
infrastructure is messier than people realize.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/4330555955_1692e554fc_o-2400x1800.jpg)Census workers
visit the State Capitol of California in Sacramento. (U.S. Census
Bureau/Flickr)

  
**The last census didn’t actually ask about citizenship; but there was so much
talk of it, and people were afraid. Did census employees tell you if the
people they met were afraid to talk to them?_— Clara, from Washington, D.C._**

In my mind, what makes the proposal to ask about citizenship terrifying is not
that people will “lie,” but that a large number of people will avoid the
census taker to begin with. They won’t fill out the forms, even if they are
citizens, because members of their household aren’t. They won’t answer the
door when the enumerators knock. The potential for an undercount is
significant.

And the Census Bureau’s researchers fully understand this, which is why
they’ve been opposed to this question since it was first proposed. They don’t
want to undercount people. But politicians might find that advantageous.

In fact, the Census Bureau [conducted lots of internal
research](https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2024/adrm/CES-
WP-24-31.html) about the citizenship question in advance of the 2020 census;
in short, the question reduces participation due to fear and lack of trust.

Other factors could also contribute to census avoidance. For example, while
ICE raids predate the second Trump administration, they are certainly going to
significantly affect how people interpret the enumerators knocking on their
door.

This suggests that fear and distrust will be a big factor in 2030. And it’s
not clear to me whether or not the Census Bureau has the resources to evaluate
how fear is going to influence the 2030 census. And keep in mind that
thousands of civil servants have been let go and hiring has been frozen, so
there are many ways in which we will be blinkered going into the 2030 census.

And while the citizenship question is front and center right now, it’s
important to recognize that the harder part of the 2020 census was that it
unfolded during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result, _many_ people
were afraid to talk with enumerators. They were afraid of government
officials; they were afraid of strangers; but they were also just afraid that
another human might spread a disease. To my knowledge, the bureau did not try
to disentangle these fears. Enumerators wore masks and did their best to
assure people that they were legitimate.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20267026743967-scaled.jpg)A Census 2020 worker helps
someone fill out a census form at an outreach event in New York. (Photo by Lev
Radin/Sipa USA)(Sipa via AP Images)

  
**Some census workers may have reported aggression toward them. Is that common
and how would that have impacted the overall process?_— @esmewrites, on
Bluesky_**

Sadly, this is more common than most people realize. Early on, when I was
talking with a census official about why it was so hard to keep enumerators
from quitting given that the pay was significantly above minimum wage, I got a
one-word answer: dogs. Apparently, getting bitten by a dog is an occupational
hazard for Amazon workers, USPS workers, and census workers. I talked with
multiple enumerators who quit after the first, second, or third dog bite.

I also talked to one who seemed to be invincible, having been bitten by more
dogs than he could remember. That doesn’t make it any less disturbing.

Enumerators encounter all sorts of unexpected and unpleasant situations.
People coming to their door naked, with a shotgun, or with a stream of hateful
words. But enumerators also encounter the best side of Americans. Enumerators
told me stories of getting to know their neighbors, being able to help an
elderly resident, and being able to create connective tissue in their towns.

The Census Bureau’s operational plan presumes that a shockingly high number of
enumerators will quit. During training, bureau officials try to prepare
enumerators for what the work is like, but they also know that no matter what
they say, many people won’t know if it’s for them until they try it out. No
amount of roleplay or training videos prepares people for what happens when
they face someone who means them harm. The Census Bureau also works hard to
identify the enumerators who seem invincible. I met one who had no problem
dropping into towns in the middle of wildfires or convincing someone to
respond even as a gun was pointed at his face. These special enumerators are
deployed to the hardest cases.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/7024455521_6b5109aa70_o-2400x1607.jpg)A person
receiving 2010 census forms in the mail. (U.S. Census Bureau/Flickr)

  
**We know that it’s so much harder to poll people these days. I’m curious if
it has become harder for the census to reach people for the American Community
Survey, and what implications that might have for its accuracy._— Aaron
Mendelson, a journalist who has extensively written on issues linked to_**[**
_redistricting_**](https://publicintegrity.org/politics/elections/who-
counts/how-one-city-ended-prison-gerrymandering/)** _and challenges of_**[**
_data gathering_**](https://www.thetrace.org/2026/04/shooting-gun-violence-
data-america-q1-2026/)** _._**

In the United States, the public is legally required to complete the census.
And that includes the American Community Survey, which was once the “long
form” that was given to only a portion of the American public during a census
and is now a rolling sample-based survey.

And now the asterisks come in. Not everyone follows the law and the Census
Bureau is not keen on using law enforcement to force compliance. So the bureau
begs and pleads and sends notices, but it also knows that there are gaps. And
so it does a lot of methodological work to leverage external data sources and
figure out how to effectively re-weight the responses to make the best data
possible, knowing full well that it would be better off if everyone just
participated. The bureau also does its best to document the total measurement
error and other limitations to its approach, although a lot of this is in the
footnotes and methodological documentation that most data users ignore.

A new asterisk has entered the playing field. In some of its internal
materials, the Trump administration has stated that, going forward, the ACS
will be optional and voluntary. If they go through with that, this is going to
create a whole new headache for the bureau.

This is definitely a ‘wait and see, but be prepared’ kind of situation. And
it’s one where Congress hasn’t been tremendously helpful. Many electeds echo
earlier politicians who opposed putting many questions on the 1790 census
[because](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8415740/) “gratifying an
idle curiosity” would be “a waste of trouble and supplying materials for idle
people to make a book.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/7024455119_63b332179f_o-
scaled.jpg)A census worker with a farmer in the 1940s. (U.S. Census
Bureau/Flickr)

  
**What are your main fears over what Trump’s team could change in the next
census? How could they hurt the census?_— Jenna, from Pennsylvania_**

My main fear is the loss of legitimacy. By nearly all scientific and
statistical measures, the quality of data produced in the 2020 census was
better than any census conducted in the 19th or 20th centuries (and the first
census in 1790). We can quibble over how it compares to the censuses in 2000
and 2010, but those censuses didn’t have to reckon with a global pandemic.
And, yet, many people are absolutely convinced that the data were crap. Why?
And what does this say about the data that we used for centuries?

The legitimacy of a census is not something that is scientifically derived; it
is rooted in our collective belief that these data are good enough for the
purposes set forth by the Constitution. But _good enough_ is socially
constructed, rooted in the social fabric and collective imaginary.

Right now, the Census Bureau is facing the destruction of long-standing norms,
the departure of people with sizable institutional knowledge, micromanaging of
the scientific method, and egregious partisan dictates. These can materially
harm the bureau’s ability to do its job, for sure. But even if the bureaucrats
manage to pull off “the impossible,” I’m worried that no one will believe them
or the data that they produce.

  
**Why do they need to break down the population by race? When I worked on the
Census in 2010 I felt it was inappropriate to ask those questions since we’re
all supposed to be equal before the law _. — @karakoy, on X  _**

This is an interesting byproduct of legislative choices made in the middle of
the 20th century. Starting in the 1960s, Congress passed numerous civil rights
laws that were designed to address discrimination in the U.S. Many of these
laws were anchored to the race categories collected by the census, including
the Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and the Equal Employment Opportunity Act of
1972. But the most important and relevant law is the Voting Rights Act (VRA)
of 1965. In an era of Jim Crow, one of the ways that states were
disenfranchising Black communities was to create hurdles for Black residents
to vote. Another way was to draw Congressional districts that would make it
impossible for the candidate that Black voters desired to ever obtain a
majority. The VRA outlawed literacy tests and other barriers to voting, but it
also ordered the states to draw districts that would allow minorities to have
access to a majority voting district if such a map was possible.

If regulators and courts don’t have trustworthy data about race in the U.S.,
it’s not possible to uphold the anti-discrimination laws that depend on these
data. This is where the census data comes in. These data are used to ensure
that minority populations cannot be systematically disenfranchised by law.

Of course, if you don’t like these laws, one way of enacting [“policymaking by
other means”](https://www.russellsage.org/publications/book/administrative-
burden) is to dismantle the data upon which they depend. This is why people
are [so outraged](https://handsoffourcens.us/) about what’s happening. While
we can have reasonable conversations about how to best understand the
demographics of a given population, what’s at stake here is the viability of
anti-discrimination laws that are anchored to these data.

For a fascinating history of the intersection of race and the census, I highly
recommend Cristina Mora’s [“Making
Hispanics,”](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/M/bo15345128.html)
Melissa Nobles’ [“Shades of
Citizenship,”](https://www.sup.org/books/politics/shades-citizenship) and Ken
Prewitt’s [“What is ‘Your’
Race?”](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691157030/what-is-
your-race)

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/4322720982_d2811f37ed_o.jpg)A mural in New York City
that features the 2010 census. (U.S. Census Bureau/Flickr)

  
**Is there time to fix the census starting in January 2029?_— @tacramp, on
Bluesky_**

No. The time is now.

Each decade, the Census Bureau updates its procedures from the previous
decades. In years ending in 6 (e.g. 2026, as in now!), the key operational
plans and residence rules are announced, and Congress has the power to reject
the proposals and demand something else. In years ending in 7, the topics of
the questions are announced. Congress could object and order the bureau to
address different questions. In years ending in 8, the final questions for the
census are announced. Once again, Congress could take action. But by January
of years ending in 9, key operations are underway, printing has begun, and the
major systems have been built and tested.

So every key component of the 2030 census will be in full production and
rollout by January 2029. This is why Congress must stop abdicating its
responsibility and ensure that the Constitution is upheld and the people are
counted. The big question in all of this is, will this Congress take action?
And, more importantly, will the Congress that’s seated after this upcoming
election take action?
